name: M*LIB (m-dict hash map, DICT_DEF2)
baseline: std::unordered_map (GNU libstdc++ STL; also std::vector, std::set, std::string in the same suite)
workload: c-stl-comparison bench: UMap U64 inserts 20,000,000 random unsigned long key/value pairs then performs 20,000,000 random lookups (about half found); the same harness also times a string-key map, a 256-byte-key map, a growing array, a sorted set and string replace. Time is best of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: EPYC 7763 run on the repo's result branch: UMap U64 M*LIB dict 923.10 ms vs STL unordered_map 11670.18 ms (12.6x, derived from page data), dict Bulk 737.57 ms (15.8x, derived), open-addressing dict 934.82 ms; UMap Str dict 815.71 ms vs STL umap 2930.79 ms (3.6x, derived); UMap Big dict 1139.77 ms vs STL umap 4185.96 ms (3.7x, derived); Seq(Array) 690.71 ms vs STL vector 1560.62 ms (2.3x, derived); SSet B+tree 813.29 ms vs STL Rbtree 2627.84 ms (3.2x, derived); String Replace 536.51 ms vs STL 1396.06 ms (2.6x, derived). Memory for UMap U64 dict 589.90M vs STL umap 933.78M. README says 'M*LIB is on par with the STL or even faster' (graphs only, GNU C++ STL v10.2).
compiler_and_flags: bench/Makefile: CFLAGS=-O2 -march=native, C built with cc -std=c11, STL side built with c++ -std=c++11 (g++, so libstdc++), each bench run with --quiet --best --repeat 3. GCC version is not in BENCH.md; the project wiki page Benchmark-result states GCC 16.1 with -O2 -march=native; the M*LIB README graphs state GNU C++ STL v10.2.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, lscpu line in BENCH.md); an i5-3210M result is also published in the repo (master branch bench/doc/BENCH.md).
tradeoffs: Pure C99/C11 header-only library that generates typed containers with preprocessor macros (oplists); explicit init/clear calls, no copy by assignment, container hands out borrowed pointers; default policy aborts the program on allocation failure (customisable); no C++ templates, exceptions or iterators in the STL sense. Sorted-set variants include a B+tree that is not API-equivalent to std::set.
caveats: Benchmark harness is the library author's own repo (P-p-H-d/c-stl-comparison), run on a shared GitHub-hosted CI VM, so timings are noisy and no CPU pinning is stated; GCC version is not printed in BENCH.md. STL rows use default std::hash (identity for integers), no reserve() and operator[] inserts, so the 12.6x U64 gap is partly default-std::unordered_map node-allocation cost, and other open-addressing C++ maps would narrow it (Boost unordered flat map is 1464.12 ms on the same page, 7.97x faster than STL; KLIB khash 1257.84 ms). M*LIB is not uniformly faster: in the same BENCH.md STL Sort is 1105.64 ms vs M*LIB Sort 1706.60 ms (STL 1.54x faster; stable sort 1237.25 vs 1285.71 ms, close) and STL SSet(Rbtree) 2627.84 ms beats M*LIB SSet(Rbtree) 3092.66 ms (the win is the B+tree). Seq(Deque) 896.94 vs 1799.15 ms and Seq(List) 971.39 vs 1193.67 ms are smaller wins. Ratios are derived from page data, not stated by the project. The M*LIB README Performance section shows only PNG graphs against GNU C++ STL v10.2, so the table above is the checkable evidence. The mlib commit pinned in BENCH.md (4acdfe4) is the current master head.

name: micron.cpp (cmemory memcpy/memset/memmove)
baseline: glibc memcpy / memset / memmove (system libc, called as ::memcpy in the harness; glibc version not stated)
workload: benches/memory_random_bench.cpp: batches of 16384 random-offset operations with SPEC2017 size and alignment distributions over a working set of 32 KiB to 1 MiB, 5 measurements, CPU pinned, cycles per byte; micron mc::memcpy/memset/memmove versus libc.
claimed_speedup: benches/results/mem_random_s2_final.csv cycles/byte micron vs libc: memcpy 0.2803 vs 0.3480 at 32768 (1.24x, derived from page data), 0.2590 vs 0.3815 at 262144 (1.47x, derived), 0.3045 vs 0.4829 at 1048576 (1.59x, derived); memset 0.2377 vs 0.4532 at 1048576 (1.91x, derived), 0.1936 vs 0.2190 at 32768 (1.13x, derived); memmove 0.3236 vs 0.4231 at 1048576 (1.31x, derived). micron is faster in all 18 rows of that file.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the CSV. Sibling result files from the same author and dates (abcmalloc_core_baseline.csv, rng_final_native.csv) state GCC 16.2.1 20260819, -O3 -march=native, built with 'duck --perf --fp --no-ssp --no-lto -i .'. The bench source adds #pragma GCC optimize(-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns).
hardware: Not stated in the CSV. Sibling result files name an Intel Core i7-5960X (Haswell-E, 8C/16T, 20 MiB L3), Linux 7.1.9-200.fc44 (Fedora 44), CPU pinned.
tradeoffs: Freestanding re-implementation of libc and the C++ standard library (no libc dependency, C++23 or C++26, x86-64 focus with an ARM32 and bare-metal branch); README states the ABI may change without notice, performance takes precedence over safety, and the code is not a drop-in for the STL ABI. abcmalloc, the bundled allocator, is MIT while the rest is BSL-1.0.
caveats: The README and docs publish no numbers; the 'must demonstrate superior performance' line is a design principle. Only the benches/results directory has data, and the only micron-versus-external-baseline rows found are memory primitives against glibc, not the allocator or STL containers named in the seed guess (allocator results are before/after against micron's own earlier revisions, and sort_bench_std.cpp, heap_bench_std.cpp and stack_bench_std.cpp have no recorded results). The claim is selective: the sibling file mem_detail_s2_final_a.csv (same author) shows libc faster overall for hot memcpy (micron wins 170 of 513 cells, geomean libc/micron cycles 0.96) and hot memmove (45 of 182, 0.89), faster on all 14 cold-cache memcpy cells (0.85) and on 11 of 14 cold memset cells, with libc far ahead at tiny sizes (for example memmove at 3 bytes 0.27 vs 1.12 cycles/byte); micron wins hot memset (222 of 386, geomean 1.12). The random-size win applies to working sets of 32 KiB and above only. First-party, single machine (Haswell-E, an older CPU than glibc's newest ifunc tuning targets), glibc version unstated, compiler and CPU absent from the cited CSV, so tier C. Ratios are derived from page data.
